title: Shutdown Crisis Looming As Newsletter Runs Out Of Words
subtitle: Both sides wrangling to milk this disaster for all it's worth
body_html:
This is the 994th post on The Frontier Psychiatrists.

However, the inner workings of such an extensive endeavor aren’t always clear to readers. One constraint on subsequent posts is simply “having enough words to say.” Readers might be thinking, “Well, it’s a newsletter—without words, am I just looking at a lame Tumblr for forrest plots and pictures of where Owen went this past weekend?”

Our words, at TFPs, are provisioned through a complex appropriations process; however. Absent compromise, further words are unlikely to be authorized. This will lead to a crisis for the newsletter and a complete shutdown of services, at least among articles that you’d want to read. To be clear, some articles I write without pay, and others are funded by service fees such as reader subscriptions.

However, many critical pieces of education and satire are, as of the looming deadline for a continuing resolution on Tuesday, apt to shut down entirely. Wherefore, sassy takes imagining a Lord of the Rings Middle-earth with gloomy and rule-bound Compliance lawyers ready to litigate over the lack of safety measures in the Mines of Moria?

Other articles are similarly at risk, including those educating readers about the adverse effects of common medications, such as the risk of weight gain from common insomnia medicines.

This article alone could have been a thrilling deep dive into the connection between literacy, economic progress, and whaling:

The ability to read, by most people, has also been a key to unlocking a better future:

“Two early exceptions to this broad trend were the Netherlands and England, which had achieved literacy rates above fifty percent of their populations by the mid-seventeenth century.”

Being able to read allowed the Brits and Dutch, and thus their colonies, like the Americans, to take advantage of reading and writing to accelerate their economic growth. And these two cohorts also aggressively pursued the “venture capital” high-risk/high-reward activities of the day more than any other cultures at the time. Yes, that is overwhelmingly whaling. There is a remarkable 3-part series on the topic done by Freakonomics, strongly recommended.

Yes, I was actually working on writing something so wonky. However, absent appropriate words? It’s not happening.

A newsletter-wide shutdown comes at a crucial juncture, at which The Frontier Psychiatrists just crossed 7,000 subscribers, and yet still lags behind leading science authors like and his brilliant “Psychiatry At The Margins.” We are falling behind, dear readers. Awais is on the rise. Now is no time for us to run out of words, and yet, here we are.

Some have encouraged a temporary fix, like a resolution to provide additional prepositions, nouns, and verbs only for the next 7 weeks:

“You can’t do this by Tuesday, and you can’t do it while you’re holding the American people hostage with a The Frontier Psychiatrists shutdown,” Senator DoNothing said on “Meet the Press.”

Others have sought to capitalize on this opportunity to advance their own agenda:

Senator Spooner, on Sunday, said there will be “huge pressure” on Readers to agree to talks to restore healthcare articles, which he said threaten to not amuse those working in rural hospitals and dramatically hike insurance premiums.

“We don’t want a shutdown,” he said on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “We hope that they sit down and have a unserious negotiation with us.”

Senate Funpublican Leader “John” has left the door open to eventually dealing with the healthcare satire, but says Congress must first pass a temporary wording bill to avert a shutdown.

I’m thrilled to have the support of Funpublicans in both the House and the Senate; however, in this case, it won’t be enough. Sixty votes are required to avert running out of things to say, and nouns and verbs alone are not enough parts of speech to craft the kinds of diverse sentences that make up The Frontier Psychiatrists columns.

Funpublicans warned the fake news media—whose words are allocated through a separate process from health-satire publications—that this kind of brinksmanship puts all of us who enjoy learning something new about TMS while having a chortle at risk:

“They’re playing with fire, and they know it,” Senator John said on Sunday.

As if to underscore the risk, he highlighted this recent wordy podcast about TMS. Then he shared some photos Owen Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, took recently, as if to underscore the horror of a wordless The Frontier Psychiatrists:

Absent captions, it’s hard to know what to make of these.

Thank you for reading—and let your elected representatives know running out of words is no laughing matter.

Maybe they even pass the S.1717 - Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2025 as part of the compromise?

Share

You can contact your senator here.

Thanks for reading. If you want to read something serious about mental health, at my day job over at Radial, we have this new blog post breaking down different kinds of depression available!

The Frontier Psychiatrists is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
